title: Collecting and describing data
calculator: Four-function calculator allowed; supplied nontrivial values.
study_note: All questions, answers, and explanations are public. Numerical examples are illustrative classroom scenarios.

questions.stem: A library surveys only people entering the library to estimate how often all students visit. What is the main concern?
questions.explanation: Selection excludes a relevant part of the population, regardless of sample size.
choices: The sample must be too small.
Randomly ordering the responses removes the concern.
Students who never visit are excluded.
Every recorded visit count is wrong.

questions.stem: A random sample of 80 enrolled students reports 30% support for later hours. Which conclusion is justified?
questions.explanation: A sample result is evidence about a population, not an exact census result.
choices: Exactly 24 students in the entire college support later hours.
Exactly 30% of all students support later hours.
30% describes the sample and estimates population support.

questions.stem: A database codes printer brands as 1, 2, and 3. Why would averaging these codes be misleading?
questions.explanation: Arithmetic on arbitrary labels does not describe a meaningful numerical quantity.
choices: The largest code is always the most common brand.
The numbers are labels; recoding them could change the mean.
Every numerical entry measures an amount.

questions.stem: Exact wait times are replaced by short, medium, and long categories. What information is lost?
questions.explanation: Ordered categories retain rank information but lose exact numerical distances.
choices: The ordering of the three categories.
The exact differences between wait times.

questions.stem: A survey records whether each student uses a service. Which summary directly answers how common use is?
questions.explanation: A yes/no question is naturally summarized by its use proportion.

source.slide_title: The terms in a proportion study

choices: The total of category labels chosen arbitrarily.
The proportion of students reporting use.

questions.stem: Campus A has 30 users among 60 students; campus B has 40 among 100. Which has the higher use rate?
questions.explanation: The rates are 50% and 40%; denominators matter.
choices: Counts alone prove campus B has the higher rate.

questions.stem: A timer reports durations to the nearest second. What follows about the underlying duration?
questions.explanation: Recording precision does not make the underlying measurement discrete.
choices: It must change only in whole seconds.
It cannot be less than one second.
It may vary continuously despite rounded records.

questions.stem: A dot plot has five dots at 2 visits and one dot at 8 visits. What does the stack at 2 mean?
questions.explanation: Each dot represents an observation; a stack records repeated values.

figure.alt: Five dots at 2 visits and one dot at 8 visits.

data.alt: Five dots at 2 visits and one dot at 8 visits.

questions.stem: Two properly drawn random samples give support rates of 42% and 47%. Which explanation is reasonable?
questions.explanation: Random sampling does not eliminate ordinary variation between samples.
choices: Random samples always have equal percentages.
Chance sampling variation can produce different rates.
The larger percentage must be the true population rate.
Different rates prove one survey was fabricated.

questions.stem: A sample's mean file size is 18 KB. The study aims to estimate the mean across all files on a server. What does 18 KB represent?
questions.explanation: A sample mean summarizes its observed files and estimates a population mean.

source.slide_title: The terms in a mean study

choices: The exact population mean regardless of selection.
An estimate based on the sampled files.
The size of every file on the server.

questions.stem: A college wants each academic program represented in a survey. Which plan best achieves that directly?
questions.explanation: Sampling within each program ensures representation from those groups.
choices: Randomly sample students within every program.
Invite only students who previously complained.
Select the first students entering one room.

questions.stem: Plan A samples students from every building. Plan B randomly chooses two buildings and surveys everyone there. What distinguishes Plan B?
questions.explanation: The second plan selects whole groups, rather than sampling within every group.
choices: It guarantees all possible student samples are equally likely.
It studies all students in selected groups.
It selects some students from every group.

questions.stem: A systematic sample starts at ID 3 and takes every tenth ID. Which IDs appear first?
questions.explanation: Add ten to the starting ID at each selection.

questions.stem: A roster repeats a ten-person pattern, with every tenth entry a team leader. Why could taking every tenth entry be problematic?
questions.explanation: Periodicity in the list can produce a systematically unrepresentative sample.
choices: A larger interval always makes selection random.
The sampling interval can align with the repeating pattern.

questions.stem: Which change best addresses a poll that includes only frequent library users?
questions.explanation: Correcting coverage is more important than enlarging the same biased sample.
choices: Collect ten times as many frequent-user responses.

questions.stem: An open online poll receives responses mainly from students strongly opposed to a fee. What is the concern?
questions.explanation: Voluntary response can overrepresent people with especially strong views.
choices: The percentage becomes exact with 100 responses.
An online survey necessarily has no data.
Willingness to respond may depend on opinion.
All random samples favor strong opinions.

questions.stem: Students are randomly invited, but only 15% respond. Which concern remains?
questions.explanation: Random invitation does not eliminate nonresponse bias.
choices: Low response proves every answer false.

questions.stem: Which wording is most neutral for a parking survey?
questions.explanation: Neutral wording avoids suggesting the desired evaluation.
choices: Do you support the proposed parking fee?
Do you oppose the helpful parking fee?
Do you support the unfair parking fee?
Why do you dislike the parking fee?

questions.stem: Students rate a service while its manager watches. Compared with anonymous responses, what might happen?
questions.explanation: Pressure or perceived consequences can influence responses.

questions.stem: A selected student's name is removed before the next random draw. What changes?
questions.explanation: Sampling without replacement prevents repeats of the selected individual.
choices: That student cannot be selected again.
The same name must be selected next.
Every remaining student becomes impossible to select.

questions.stem: Students choosing tutoring score higher. Why is a causal claim uncertain?
questions.explanation: A self-selected comparison can mix tutoring effects with other differences.
choices: Motivation may affect both tutoring attendance and scores.
A larger score difference removes all confounding.
Any score difference proves a tutoring effect.

questions.stem: Volunteers are randomly assigned to two practice formats. What does random assignment primarily help with?
questions.explanation: Random assignment helps support causal comparisons; it does not ensure population representativeness.
choices: Eliminating the need to measure outcomes.
Guaranteeing identical scores in both groups.
Balancing other influences between treatment groups.

questions.stem: Randomly assigned groups have slightly different initial mean scores. What follows?
questions.explanation: Random assignment balances influences in expectation, not perfectly in each experiment.
choices: Random assignment requires exact matching of every score.
Chance imbalance can occur despite random assignment.
The study must have used a census.

questions.stem: One teacher uses format A and another uses format B. Why is a score difference hard to attribute?
questions.explanation: The design cannot separate teacher differences from format differences.
choices: Teacher and format effects are mixed together.
There are too many treatment groups to compare.
Different teachers guarantee format A is better.

questions.stem: A grader does not know which practice format each paper's author used. What problem does this reduce?
questions.explanation: Blinding the grader reduces assessment bias tied to treatment knowledge.
choices: Students being absent from the population.

questions.stem: A printer study uses only one printer per paper type. Why is that weak evidence?
questions.explanation: Replication helps distinguish treatment effects from variation among units.
choices: Two observations guarantee a representative result.
Printer-specific differences may dominate the comparison.
Replication would eliminate all possible errors.
Paper type cannot affect printer performance.

questions.stem: Everyone tries format A first and format B second. What could explain better second scores besides format B?
questions.explanation: Order and practice can be confounded with format.
choices: A guarantee of equal prior knowledge.
The lack of any treatment order.

questions.stem: A well-run randomized experiment finds better results for an app among its volunteers. Which claim needs extra caution?
questions.explanation: Generalization depends on the volunteers and setting, beyond random assignment.
choices: The observed volunteers had different average results.
Random assignment helped compare the formats.
The study provides evidence about an app effect in this setting.
The same effect applies to all students everywhere.

questions.stem: A researcher deletes genuine results that disagree with the desired conclusion. What is the problem?
questions.explanation: Valid observations cannot be discarded merely because they are unfavorable.
choices: The report no longer fairly represents the collected evidence.
A smaller dataset guarantees less bias.
Deleting inconvenient values always improves accuracy.
Any unusual observation is automatically an error.

questions.stem: A public dataset includes names beside individual survey answers. Which change best protects privacy while preserving group summaries?
questions.explanation: De-identification can preserve useful aggregate evidence while reducing identification risks.
choices: Keep names and omit the study methods.
Replace every answer with the overall mean.

questions.stem: Frequencies for 0, 1, 2, and 3 jobs are 2, 3, 4, and 1. How many sessions had at most 1 job?
questions.explanation: At most 1 includes the frequencies for both 0 and 1.

questions.stem: A table has positive frequency at exactly 2 jobs. How do counts for fewer than 2 and at most 2 compare?
questions.explanation: At most includes the observations equal to the cutoff.
choices: At most 2 has the larger count.
Neither can be found from exact frequencies.
Fewer than 2 has the larger count.

questions.stem: A cumulative table gives 30% below 5 seconds and 75% below 10 seconds. What percent is from 5 to less than 10?
questions.explanation: Subtract cumulative percentages at the two boundaries.

questions.stem: Four mutually exclusive, exhaustive categories have reported proportions 0.20, 0.30, 0.40, and 0.25. What needs checking?
questions.explanation: Exhaustive nonoverlapping categories must have total probability or relative frequency 1.

questions.stem: Three reported percentages are 33.3%, 33.3%, and 33.3%. What most reasonably explains the 99.9% total?
questions.explanation: Rounding can make displayed percentages differ slightly from 100%.

questions.stem: A grouped table reports 12 durations from 5 to less than 10 seconds. Can it tell exactly how many equal 7 seconds?
questions.explanation: Grouping preserves interval counts but loses individual values.
choices: No; exact positions within the interval are hidden.

questions.stem: Ratings poor, fair, good, excellent are coded 1 through 4. What is safest to infer from the codes?
questions.explanation: Ordered categories establish rank, not equal measurement distances.
choices: Each adjacent rating differs by exactly one unit of satisfaction.
Excellent ranks above good, but equal numerical gaps are not established.
Excellent is exactly twice as favorable as fair.

questions.stem: A room at 20 degrees Celsius is compared with one at 10 degrees Celsius. Which statement is justified?
questions.explanation: Celsius supports meaningful differences but its zero is not an absolute zero.
choices: The first is 10 degrees warmer on that scale.
The first is twice as comfortable for every person.
The first has twice the absolute temperature.

questions.stem: Students may use both laptops and tablets. Laptop use is 70%, tablet use 60%. Why is a two-slice pie chart inappropriate?
questions.explanation: Pie slices partition a whole; overlapping memberships are not such a partition.
choices: A pie chart requires exactly three categories.

questions.stem: Service A has 10 complaints in 100 jobs; B has 20 in 400 jobs. Which has the lower complaint rate?
questions.explanation: The rates are 5% for B and 10% for A.
choices: The service with fewer complaints must have the lower rate.

questions.stem: A stemplot key says stem 2, leaf 5 means 25 KB. Stem 3 has leaves 0, 2, 2. Which values does it show?
questions.explanation: The key supplies place value and repeated leaves represent repeated observations.

questions.stem: A stemplot includes an empty stem 2 between stems 1 and 3. What does that show?
questions.explanation: An empty stem preserves a visible gap on the numerical scale.
choices: There are no values in the twenties.

questions.stem: Two stemplots use different keys: one leaf unit is 1 second, the other 10 seconds. What must happen before comparing spreads visually?
questions.explanation: Visual widths are comparable only after accounting for scale.
choices: Assume equal stem lengths imply equal spread.
Count only the number of stems.
Account for the different numerical scales.

questions.stem: Histogram bins are [0,5), [5,10), [10,15). Where does a duration of exactly 5 belong?
questions.explanation: The left endpoint is included and the right endpoint excluded.

questions.stem: Histogram counts are 3 in [0,5), 7 in [5,10), and 2 in [10,15). How many values are below 10?
questions.explanation: The first two bins contain all values below 10.

questions.stem: A histogram is rebuilt using wider bins. What is likely lost?
questions.explanation: Wider bins combine neighboring values and smooth small features.
choices: The numerical nature of the variable.
The need for an axis scale.
Fine detail such as small gaps and local peaks.

questions.stem: Daily print totals are shown in a histogram instead of a time-series graph. What information is lost?
questions.explanation: A histogram summarizes the distribution without retaining chronology.
choices: Which total occurred on which date.

questions.stem: A bar graph of counts 98 and 100 starts its vertical axis at 97. What impression might it exaggerate?
questions.explanation: A truncated baseline can make a small count difference appear visually large.
choices: The size of the difference between the counts.

questions.stem: Categories in a bar graph are reordered alphabetically. What changes?
questions.explanation: Changing categorical order does not change the observations.
choices: The number of observations in each category.
The display order, but not category frequencies.

questions.stem: Histogram bins have unequal widths but equal counts. Why can equal raw-count bar heights mislead about concentration?
questions.explanation: With unequal widths, density scaling is needed for area to represent frequency fairly.
choices: Every histogram must be a time series.
Wider bins always contain smaller values.
The wider bin spreads its count over more numerical space.

questions.stem: The ordered data are 2, 4, 4, 7, 20. What is the median?
questions.explanation: The middle observation is the third value, 4.

questions.stem: The ordered data are 1, 3, 5, 9. What is the median?
questions.explanation: Average the two middle values, 3 and 5.

questions.stem: A score is reported at approximately the 90th percentile. What kind of information does that give?
questions.explanation: A percentile describes relative position, not percentage correct. This question does not require an exact rank, tie rule, or interpolation convention.
choices: That 90% of exam answers were correct.
Its position relative to other scores.

questions.stem: Q1 is 8 and Q3 is 14. What does the interval 8 to 14 describe approximately?
questions.explanation: Quartiles bound approximately the middle 50%, with ties and conventions affecting exact counts.

questions.stem: Using the reported quartiles, group A has Q1=3, Q3=9; group B has Q1=10, Q3=14. Which has greater IQR?
questions.explanation: Use the reported quartiles: the IQRs are 9-3=6 and 14-10=4. No choice of quartile algorithm is required.
choices: The larger median must determine the IQR.

questions.stem: A basic box plot reports minimum 0, Q1=2, median 3, Q3=4, maximum 20. Which comparison is supported?
questions.explanation: Using the displayed summary, the upper segment spans 20-4=16 units and the lower segment spans 2-0=2 units. Segment length describes numerical spread, not an exact observation count; quartile conventions and ties can affect those counts.
choices: The plot establishes the exact mean.
The lower segment contains no observations.
The upper segment must contain three times as many observations.
The segment from Q3 to the maximum spans a wider numerical range than the segment from the minimum to Q1.

figure.alt: Basic box plot: minimum 0, Q1 2, median 3, Q3 4, maximum 20. Whiskers show min and max.

data.alt: Basic box plot: minimum 0, Q1 2, median 3, Q3 4, maximum 20. Whiskers show min and max.

questions.stem: A box plot has median 6. Can it reveal exactly how many observations equal 5?
questions.explanation: A box plot compresses the data into a few summary positions.
choices: No; the summary does not retain those exact counts.

questions.stem: Two datasets have identical five-number summaries. What follows?
questions.explanation: Five summary values do not determine all observations.
choices: Their sample sizes must be identical.
They can still have different internal distributions.

questions.stem: Two reasonable quartile methods give upper outlier fences of 18 and 20 for the same dataset. One observation is 35. Which conclusion agrees with both methods?
questions.explanation: The value 35 is well above both reported fences, so choosing between these conventions does not change the flag. An outlier flag alone does not establish a recording error.
choices: Only the method with fence 18 flags the observation.
The observation is not flagged under either method.
The observation must be a recording error.
The observation is flagged as unusually high under both methods.

questions.stem: A modified box plot marks 30 as a separate high outlier. Its upper whisker ends at 18. What does 18 represent?
questions.explanation: Modified whiskers end at observed nonoutlier values; the outlier remains part of the data.
choices: The upper fence whether observed or not.
The largest observed value not flagged as an outlier.

questions.stem: For 2, 3, 3, 4, 18, how does the mean compare with the median?
questions.explanation: The high value pulls the mean above the median of 3.
choices: No comparison is possible without a calculator.

questions.stem: In 2, 3, 3, 4, 18, the 18 is replaced by 180. What happens?
questions.explanation: The middle position stays the same while the total increases greatly.
choices: The mean increases; the median stays 3.
The median increases more than the mean.

questions.stem: Most files are small, with a few extremely large files. Which better describes a typical file's size?
questions.explanation: The median is less pulled by a few large files.

questions.stem: A frequency table lists 1 page for 8 jobs and 5 pages for 2 jobs. Why is (1+5)/2 inappropriate for mean pages per job?
questions.explanation: A per-job mean must weight values by their frequencies.
choices: It ignores how often each value occurs.
It counts too many individual jobs.
It gives extra weight to 1-page jobs.

questions.stem: Ten jobs average 2 pages; thirty jobs average 6 pages. Where is the combined mean?
questions.explanation: The larger group has more weight in the combined mean.

questions.stem: Four jobs have a mean of 5 pages. What is the total number of pages?
questions.explanation: Total equals number of observations times their mean.

questions.stem: Every recorded duration increases by 3 seconds. What happens to the mean and median?
questions.explanation: A common additive shift moves both centers by that amount.

questions.stem: Every size is converted from MB to KB using 1 MB=1,000 KB. What happens to the mean's numerical value?
questions.explanation: A unit conversion scales every observation and its mean equally.

questions.stem: A mean is estimated from grouped intervals using midpoints. Why is it generally approximate?
questions.explanation: Grouping hides exact values, so midpoint weighting replaces them with approximations.
choices: Frequencies cannot be used in means.
The sample size is necessarily unknown.
Actual observations need not equal the interval midpoints.

questions.stem: A dataset has mean 10. One new observation equal to 10 is added. What happens to the mean?
questions.explanation: Adding a value equal to the current mean preserves that mean.

questions.stem: Data are 0, 8, 9, 9, 10. Which center is lower?
questions.explanation: The isolated low value pulls the mean below the median of 9.

questions.stem: Most waits are short, but a few extend far toward large values. What determines the skew direction?
questions.explanation: Skew is named for the direction of the long tail.
choices: The side with the tallest bar alone.
The long tail toward large values.

questions.stem: Data are 2, 4, 6, 8, 10. How do mean and median compare?
questions.explanation: The values balance symmetrically around 6.
choices: The mean is below the median.

questions.stem: A distribution has equal peaks near 2 and 8 and is symmetric around 5. What follows?
questions.explanation: A symmetric distribution can be bimodal with its center between peaks.
choices: Symmetry does not require a single peak.

questions.stem: Add 10 to every value in a right-skewed dataset. What happens to its shape?
questions.explanation: Translation moves locations without changing shape.

questions.stem: Remove 100 from 1, 2, 3, 4, 100. What happens to the mean and median?
questions.explanation: The mean changes from 22 to 2.5; the median changes from 3 to 2.5.
choices: The mean increases and median decreases.
The median increases and mean stays unchanged.
Both decrease, with a much larger decrease in the mean.

questions.stem: Data 4, 5, 6 become 4, 5, 60. What happens to spread?
questions.explanation: Moving one endpoint far away increases both overall range and squared deviations.
choices: Range and standard deviation both increase.

questions.stem: Someone claims mean > median is a universal proof that any dataset is right-skewed. What is the best response?
questions.explanation: Shape and centers are related, but the ordering alone is not a universal shape theorem.
choices: It is a useful common pattern, not a universal characterization.
It proves every observation exceeds the median.
It proves the dataset is normal.

questions.stem: A recorded file size is far above the rest. What should happen before deleting it?
questions.explanation: An unusual value can be valid and informative; deletion needs a defensible reason.
choices: Keep it only if the mean equals the median.
Delete it because all outliers are mistakes.
Check whether it is an error or a genuine unusual file.

questions.stem: Notebook colors are blue, blue, black, red. Which statement meaningfully summarizes a typical category?
questions.explanation: A most-common category is meaningful without arbitrary arithmetic on labels.
choices: Blue is the most common color.
The standard deviation of color names is 1.

questions.stem: Compare 4, 5, 6 with 1, 5, 9. Which statement is correct?
questions.explanation: Both center at 5; the second has observations farther from the center.
choices: They have equal means, but the second has more spread.
The second has a larger mean.

questions.stem: A dataset's standard deviation is zero. What must be true?
questions.explanation: Zero spread requires identical values, which need not be zero.

questions.stem: Add 7 seconds to every duration. What happens to standard deviation?
questions.explanation: Distances from the shifted mean stay the same.

questions.stem: Multiply every observation by 3. What happens to standard deviation?
questions.explanation: Standard deviation scales like the observations; variance scales by the square.

questions.stem: Durations are in seconds. Which units belong to variance and standard deviation, respectively?
questions.explanation: Variance averages squared distances; standard deviation takes the square root.

questions.stem: Why is adding signed deviations from the sample mean unsuitable as a spread measure?
questions.explanation: Signed deviations sum to zero even when observations are widely spread.
choices: It necessarily counts each value twice.
The mean is always the largest value.

questions.stem: A sample has 8 observations. Its sum of squared deviations is already supplied. Which divisor gives sample variance?
questions.explanation: Sample variance uses n-1, unlike the population calculation with all population members.

questions.stem: A file is 60 KB; its group has mean 50 KB and SD 5 KB. How far above the mean is it?
questions.explanation: The difference is 10 KB, or twice the 5 KB standard deviation.

questions.stem: Score A is 10 above its mean with SD 5; score B is 12 above its mean with SD 12. Which is relatively farther above its group mean?
questions.explanation: A is 2 SD above its mean; B is 1 SD above.
choices: The larger raw score difference always wins.

questions.stem: Two services have mean wait 10 minutes, but SDs 1 and 6 minutes. What does the larger SD suggest?
questions.explanation: Standard deviation describes variation around a center, not an extra amount added to it.
choices: Every wait is six minutes longer.
Waits vary more around the same mean.
The mean must actually be 16 minutes.

questions.stem: Box plot A has median 12, IQR 4; B has median 9, IQR 8. Which statement is supported?
questions.explanation: The summaries compare centers and middle spreads, not every pair of observations.
choices: Every value in A exceeds every value in B.
B has higher median and smaller spread.
A has lower median and larger spread.
A has higher median and smaller middle-half spread.

figure.alt: Basic box plots: A has median 12 and IQR 4; B has median 9 and IQR 8. Whiskers show min and max.

data.alt: Basic box plots: A has median 12 and IQR 4; B has median 9 and IQR 8. Whiskers show min and max.

questions.stem: Every value in a dataset increases by 5. What happens to the IQR?
questions.explanation: Both quartiles shift by 5, so their difference is unchanged.

questions.stem: Datasets share min=0 and max=100, but have different IQRs. What follows?
questions.explanation: Range uses endpoints while IQR uses quartile positions.
choices: Equal ranges do not imply equal middle-half spread.
Their standard deviations must be identical.

questions.stem: All ten observations equal 5, so their median is 5. Are exactly half strictly below the median?
questions.explanation: Ties mean a median need not have half the values strictly below it.
choices: Yes; every median splits strict inequalities equally.
No; a median cannot exist with ties.
No; none are strictly below it.

questions.stem: Digital purchases rise from 40 of 100 to 60 of 200. What happened?
questions.explanation: The counts rise from 40 to 60 while shares fall from 40% to 30%.
choices: The count rose, but the share fell.
The count fell, but the share rose.

questions.stem: A bell-shaped distribution has mean 20 and SD 2. Approximately which interval contains 95%?
questions.explanation: The empirical rule uses about two standard deviations on each side for a bell-shaped distribution.

questions.stem: A distribution's shape is unknown. Which claim about the fraction within 2 SD is justified by Chebyshev's bound?
questions.explanation: Chebyshev gives a general lower bound; the empirical rule needs an appropriate bell shape.
choices: At least 75%, assuming a finite nonzero variance.

questions.stem: A sample variance is 9 minutes squared. What is its standard deviation?
questions.explanation: Standard deviation is the square root of variance and returns to the original units.

questions.stem: A dataset has mean 8. One observation below 8 is removed. What happens to the mean of the remaining values?
questions.explanation: Removing a below-average observation raises the remaining average.

questions.stem: A box plot flags an unusually large print job. Which conclusion is warranted?
questions.explanation: An outlier flag identifies unusual position under a rule, not its cause.
choices: The value must be deleted before any summary.
The job deserves investigation; the plot alone does not prove error.
The rest of the data must be normal.

alignment.basis: Existing section slides, original adapted questions; computational load intentionally reduced.
